subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF EXTENSION OF TERM OF OFFICE

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF EXTENSION OF TERM OF OFFICE
speechtext:
I should like to announce that Her Majesty the Queen has been graciously pleased to approve the continuance in office of General the Right Honourable Georges Philias Vanier as Governor General of Canada for a further and additional period of one year from the autumn of 1964. This extension of the Governor General's term is a recognition of the dedicated and distinguished manner in which General Vanier has carried out the high responsibilities of his vice regal office. I am sure the Canadian people will welcome the extension which the Governor General has indicated his willingness to accept, and the fact that His Excellency's health makes it possible for him to undertake this responsibility for a further period.
One of the happiest aspects of the extension of the term of General Vanier is that it will mean the continued presence in Rideau Hall of Madame Vanier, whose grace and charm and warmth has so endeared her to Canadians.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF EXTENSION OF TERM OF OFFICE
speechtext: While the cabinet approves the recommendation of a governor general to the Crown, this is one of the prerogatives, as it were, which rests with the Prime Minister. In 1959, I recommended to the Queen that General Vanier was the most outstanding Canadian with the qualifications for the responsibilities which would be his as Governor General of Canada and, as such, the representative of Her Majesty. The intervening years have shown that in the discharge of his duties and in the exercise of his authority General Vanier has acted with greatness, with wisdom, with distinction and, in association with Madame Vanier, with grace. They have honoured the positions they occupy, and I congratulate the government on extending the term of office.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF EXTENSION OF TERM OF OFFICE
speechtext:
The willingness of His Excellency Governor General Vanier to remain in his present position for another year will be hailed with enthusiasm by people in all parts of this country. It has been my privilege to have met all the governors general from Lord Tweedsmuir to the present day, and I know of none more popular or more highly respected than the present Governor General, and what I say with respect to him applies equally to Madame Vanier, who is greatly beloved in this country.
I am sure all members of the house will express the hope that His Excellency will enjoy good health throughout the balance of this addition to his term.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF EXTENSION OF TERM OF OFFICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure there is no single matter on which we in this house and all Canadians will join so unitedly in expressing our pleasure as the fact that Governor General Vanier has been invited to accept and has accepted the responsibility of an additional term of office as Governor General of Canada. All of us who have had the privilege of knowing the Governor General and Madame Vanier personally understand in a special way, I am sure, just how well they have fitted into their responsibilities and have drawn to this office the united support of the Canadian people. I am sure, also, that the Governor General and Madame Vanier are equally loved by those who have not had this privilege.
I believe that the general acceptance of the conference on the family, which they personally sponsored, is indicative of the tremendous good will they have engendered and the tremendous importance of the position they hold at this time as a unifying force in Canada.
Therefore, on behalf of our party and personally, I join in extending congratulations to the Prime Minister for approving the extension of their term of office, and send our best wishes and love to the Governor General and Madame Vanier.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF EXTENSION OF TERM OF OFFICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives us great pleasure to join with the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) in

Inquiries of the Ministry paying tribute to the Governor General oi Canada, General Vanier, who has accepted to continue in his high position for another year.
Mr. and Mrs. Vanier have been a credit to Canada since they have been filling their important functions, that is, since 1959. Every Canadian, both English speaking and French speaking, is proud of them. They have visited our country from east to west and north to south, and everywhere they have won the affection of all right-thinking Canadians.
Our group wishes them good health and a great deal of happiness.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Monday, July 20, consideration in committee of Bill No.

C-110, to facilitate the making of loans to students-Mr. Gordon-Mr. Lamoureux in the chair.

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, to continue with the remarks I was making last night,
I would like to deal with some of the comments made yesterday by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) in his rather vitriolic speech.
In a nutshell here is what he says: "There has been enough talk, let us take a vote on the bill. If you are not satisfied with the bill, vote against it; if you are, vote for it, so that the bill can be passed and all the students benefit by it".
In other words, since the majority in the house will vote in favour of the bill, it means that the majority will outnumber those upholding the constitutional right.
It also means that the majority will be able to violate the rights of the minority when the vote is taken.
I wonder if this is the type of co-operation which the hon. member for Port Arthur has been claiming for some time between the two great races which have built this country.
In my opinion before voting on such a bill we should have at least the time to express our views and try, if possible, to have the bill amended so that it may satisfy everyone. That is the least a people living under a democratic system could ask for.
This problem brings up the whole matter of the foundation of confederation.
If there is a field where the intrusion of the federal government is unwanted, it is in the educational field. When the federal government tries to intrude in that field, I maintain and repeat that this is a provocation of the French Canadian minority in the country, whose rights were embodied in the constitution of 1867.
Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) mentioned that the province of Quebec had made known its intention not to take advantage of this legislation, but it has been said right after that the province of Quebec will receive alternative payments under section 12 of Bill No. C-110.
In other words, Ottawa will levy taxes in the province of Quebec, like elsewhere, and will charitably turn over a certain sum of money to that province so that it can set up its own system. The federal government will still be controlling the sources of income through which the province of Quebec can develop its own educational system, so that if, at
Loans to Students
any time Ottawa wants to deprive the province of Quebec of its sources of income nothing can prevent it from doing so.
The alternative payments mentioned in Bill No. C-110 actually are tantamount to a charitable donation given by the federal government to the province of Quebec and to the provinces unwilling to take advantage of this legislation.
We want the province of Quebec to be able to levy itself the taxes it needs in order to meet the obligations it would have to assume if it were itself to implement Bill No. C-110.
In that respect, the Minister of Finance replies that it would be a difficult implementation because the amounts granted to the provinces, for tax deductions, would be extremely small, about $700,000, which would hardly be equivalent to one tenth of 1 per cent of the personal income tax.
Some contend that it is better to take compensation payments because the amount is extremely small. Here is my answer to the Minister of Finance: whether the amount be small or large, this is for us a matter of principle. We do not want the federal government to levy taxes and hand them over to the province of Quebec, to enable it to act in the field of education. We believe that the province of Quebec must collect its own taxes, whatever they amount to, and use them in the field of education.
If it is agreed for $700,000 because it is a small amount, it can be agreed as well for $1 million, because it is still a small amount, it can be agreed for $2 million because it is also a small amount compared to the federal government's budget of $6.5 billion; it can be agreed for $3 million because it is less than 1 per cent of the budget, for $5 million because it is still less than 1 per cent of personal income taxes. At that rate, when will an amount be small or big? That will be left to the discretion of the Minister of Finance, and the province of Quebec will keep on losing the control and jurisdiction it should have in the field of education.
It is then a question of principle, because even though we are told that the province of Quebec does not share in the benefits of Bill No. C-110, it falls within its scope, since it has to comply with the provisions of section 12 of that bill concerning alternative payments.
The province of Quebec may be allowed to borrow directly under the authority of the federal government but its government will

Loans to Students
be bound by the bill as it will have to "take advantage" of section 12.
That is the reason why we think section 12 should be amended. No mention should be made of alternative payments and this section should be altogether replaced by a fiscal abatement consistent with the amount the province of Quebec would pay if it were setting up its own loan plan.
These, Mr. Chairman, are the fundamentals of this bill.
If we accept today that principles be broken because the amount involved is insignificant, it would be impossible to know when the federal government would stop when greater amounts are involved, and it will have opened another door for its activity in the field of education.
Moreover, the Minister of Finance stated himself that there are nine fields of activity in which the federal government acts directly with respect to education. Considering the figures mentioned by the Minister of Finance yesterday, it becomes obvious that the federal government pays $500 million-half a billion-for educational purposes throughout the country.
There is another point that justifies our opposition not to the principle of education or of the development of education in this country, but to the intrusion of the federal government in the development of our educational system, and it is that the more measures there will be on the part of the federal government in those fields, the more obstacles and limits we will have as regards the development of an over-all plan for the extension of education under a single authority in the province of Quebec. The more authorities there will be, federal, provincial or others, to interfere in the educational field, the less opportunities there will be of unifying the development of an over-all plan so as to create a real educational system in the different provinces.
To ensure co-ordination of efforts in that field, the authority must rest with the same government; now, according to the constitution, education comes under the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces.
Another objection I have against the bill as it stands now is that the objective that we must strive to attain in the field of education is that anyone, from first graders to graduates, who has the necessary qualifications should be able to get the degree of training he wishes to have regardless of the social status or the financial means of his family. It is not by burdening students with debts or by putting them at the mercy of bank 
managers that we will reach that end. We will be successful in our endeavours only if we try to set up free education in the provinces, so that our educational establishments may be within the reach of all.
I know very well that free education is perhaps not the term we should use. It may be free for the pupil and for the student. But in the last instance, there will always be someone who has to pay for it. If it is not the pupil, it will be the parents through taxation. If not the parents, then, under the new credit system we advocate, it will be paid by the development of our natural resources. Those resources will create new credit, which will be paid to help the development of education in the various provinces.
It nevertheless remains that everybody in the various provinces should have access to the universities, colleges and technical schools, and even primary schools.
This free education and this development of education involve more than the possibility of entering university. They involve also the maintenance of the students because, when parents have no means of supporting them they nevertheless have to live, they must have means of living during their courses. Books are also involved, and the building of educational institutions, because, at the rate things are going, more and more young people look to the colleges, technical schools and universities. It is easy to realize that, for several years, there will be a need to build schools, colleges and universities, to give to everybody, not only financial but also physical access to those educational institutions which are necessary if our young people are to pursue their studies.
To give our young people financial means is not everything; they must also have facilities and teachers. At the rate things are going, there is a great and even a serious danger that facilities will not be sufficient, that there will not be enough teachers and physical facilities to enable everybody to have access to education.
That is why I say that this bill not only violates the principles of the Canadian constitution, but that it is contrary to the philosophy that, when you help someone, you do not take advantage of circumstances to push him into debt. Also, the bill is far from complete. We might say that it constitutes a weak promotional statement in the field of education.
For all these reasons we think that Bill No. C-110 should be amended, but specially section 12. That section should be amended

in order to change alternative payments for a formula which would enable the provinces, the province of Quebec in particular because that province demands respect of its rights in the field of education, for a formula, as I say, which would replace alternative payments by an equivalent fiscal abatement. Even if the amount is a small or trivial amount, it will safeguard the principle, and we should therefore take the trouble of amending that section 12, because once the principle is violated, even if it is for a small amount, then il will be a lot easier for the federal government to violate the full rights of the provinces in the field of education.
It would be possible to amend all that. I hope that the minister will be broadminded enough to accept and introduce amendments that will satisfy every group in Canada.
I say and I repeat that intrusions such as this defy and provoke openly those who complain that the federal government wants to centralize everything and take away the rights of the minorities. We do not want to be regarded as a minority in this country. Instead we want to be equal partners within the confederation. Mr. Chairman, we heard a good deal during the course of the previous stage of the debate on the desirability of a university education. I have not had the opportunity of speaking before, and I have a few remarks I should like to address to the committee within the narrower confines of the discussion on the first clause of the bill.
I am reminded of a lot of the things that have been said in regard to university education, and I hope I will not be considered altogether too cynical when I say that many members might as well have said they were against sin and in favour of motherhood, and so on. We have heard a lot of platitudes in regard to the desirability of a university education, but I do think there is a place for it in the over-all educational pattern of the country.
I have been told by some of my friends in industry that far too often we approach the problem of advanced education in this country from the wrong point of view; that far too many people are having to go to engineering schools, for instance, who would be far better qualified for their purposes in later life if they had opportunities at technical schools. In other words we are putting through university high grade technicians. We also know that a number of people go to universities who frankly are not of university calibre, and there should be a greater screening of those who desire to go there.
As has been indicated by previous speakers, particularly by my colleague the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings following the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition at the resolution stage, I think the bill attacks the problem in the wrong way in so far as assisting education is concerned. We know that the universities of this country need help now in trying to do something about the student population explosion they will face within the next decade or 15 years. Yet what we are doing is trying to push more people through facilities that are too limited both as to professorial staff and as to plant. All we are doing is expanding the size and number of classes and diluting the value of the education that may be obtained from a university.
I would have thought it far better for the federal government, the provinces and the private universities to get together on a really thorough-going plan for the provision

of more building facilities and the necessary university teachers. To my mind this is where the emphasis should have been placed. I would wager that throughout the various provinces today there are very few students with the required get up and go, the desire and the necessary academic qualifications who cannot go to university. I have had a rather keen interest in this regard, and from long study of the desirability of getting more people into the universities I find that the student who really wants to go, can go.
I will admit there are odd occasions when this is not the case, but let us not be told that there are hundreds and thousands of young people who are precluded from going to university today by reason of the fact that they lack the funds. Oh, maybe life is not as sweet for them, maybe it is not as free and easy in some cases as they might like, but I have always felt that a university degree that was well earned was all the more appreciated. I am not saying that students should have to go to university in rags or have to live on water and a crust of bread. Far be it from that. But on the other hand there is such a thing as killing with kindness. Perhaps some people think I am a little bit ice-aged in this regard, but frankly I feel that what is earned is far more appreciated and put to far better use than something handed out on a platter.
Having made those remarks I say this bill has all the good intentions in the world, but the road to hell is paved with good intentions. As I have said, this program places the wrong emphasis, and the federal government, if it must get into the field of education-and there are quite reasonable protestations that it should not get into it directly-can work in other directions. If the provincial authorities and the private universities are facing national educational problems, surely there is a way of dealing with them on the basis of plant. The previous administration facilitated the construction of residences for students and other buildings through Central Mortgage and Housing. There is much to be said in favour of that approach. I think there is much more required in providing adequate salaries for more teachers. There is a crying need to encourage the training of more teachers at the post-secondary academic level.
Let us look at the effect of this bill. I do not know whether the minister has actually consulted with his colleague the minister of defence, and in particular with the Associate Minister of National Defence, because I have a strong suspicion that this may knock the 
R.O.T.P. right on the head. I have a strong feeling what the answer will be if the average young man is faced with the prospect of an offer to lend him $5,000 over a period of years, and another offer to pay his tuition and certain expenses provided he gives four years' military service immediately after graduating.

Simple mathematics show that 24 of them dropped out, and they had to drop out into non-graduate occupations.

We should be careful. I cannot go along with the idea that we should lend this money to everybody who wants to enter university. He promised free education to all students of the province of Quebec, and nothing else.
He was elected in 1960 and the Quebec government was to establish a system of free education at all levels: university, technical, secondary, everywhere. But we know what kind of free education we have obtained to date in the province of Quebec. While we used to pay $40 or $45 per month to put our children through school, today, with free education in the province of Quebec, it costs between $85 and $90 per month. That is the whole difference between the time when we paid for the education of our children and the time when we obtained free education. Who benefits by this free education? The bureaucracy of the province of Quebec. Mr. Jean Lesage decided to champion the autonomy of the province and the rights of the provinces. Quebec will participate in the federal student loan plan.
Mr. Lesage started off like a lion and, today, he is acting more and more like a lamb when he has to face Ottawa and federal government proposals. We now have a pretty good idea of his policy of grandeur, for he is acting in an underhand manner and in no other way. In the open, it sounds great to speak of a "policy of grandeur", but what is Mr. Lesage's attitude before this bill? He simply says that he will take part in this program. That is not the solution we suggest. We suggest a system of scholarships for students and free education. That is what we have asked for, and we still ask the federal government to put the Bank of Canada at the disposal of the provinces, not to control but to serve the provinces, learning and education, and to

allow our children to acquire the knowledge they need and wish to obtain. This should be done with the credit granted by the Bank of Canada.
That is precisely what the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue (Mr. Martineau) failed to understand yesterday. He does not understand today, and he will never understand how the Bank of Canada credit could be used.
However, everybody understood that fact in 1939, when we had, for instance, to finance war operations at the outset. In 1939, the Canadian government, under the leadership of Mr. King, called upon the good services of the Bank of Canada and ordered the creation of $200 million to set up an army.
Mr. Chairman, it was possible then to call upon the Bank of Canada. Why today, for the education of our children, is it no longer possible to call upon the same services of the Bank of Canada, to use it and order it to make financially possible what is physically feasible in our country?
Then, the autonomy of every province would be respected. Mr. Chairman, the education of our children is a more important matter than that of the government, of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) or of the Quebec provincial government. Mr. Chairman, such a way of dealing with the people may have been helpful for a certain number of years, it may still help for a few years to come, but it will not help forever. Soon he will have to give an account to the people, and the people get tired of being taxed, taxed again and surtaxed. Even this legislation will involve new taxes, and part of those taxes will be redistributed to the province of Quebec as compensation payments. Once again, that is the system of crumbs at the service of the provinces controlled by the centralizing federal policy.
Mr. Chairman, we agree to the principle of the bill which is to help the students, but we do not agree at all with the yoke and everything else imposed upon the students. I hold the government of the province of Quebec fully responsible for the fact that the

federal government, after promising loans without interest to students now proposes loans bearing interest, six months after the students have graduated, because it is then that they will start paying interest on the capital borrowed. But in the province of Quebec, Mr. Lesage had promised free education at all levels, and we remind him about that from here, in Ottawa, in the House of Commons, and we advise him to keep his promises to the students of the province of Quebec, not by giving them an opportunity to run into debt, to sink a little further but by giving them the means to become gradually freer men and to acquire science and knowledge they are entitled to like the students in other provinces. That is possible without infringing on the freedom or the autonomy of the other provinces. I am in favour of respect for the autonomy of all Canadian provinces, but on condition that the autonomy of the province of Quebec is respected by the premier of that province. He sat here for many years; then he should take his responsibilities and give the students what he promised them, namely free tuition at all levels of education.

Mr. Chairman, the voters of the county of Quebec South and among them the students of Laval University, entrusted me, in 1962, with a Canadian mandate. The first implication of this mandate is, therefore, to look after the welfare of all Canadians and to discuss legislation in parliament from the point of view of their common interest.
This implies, first of all, the respect for the rights of the provinces and the rights of minorities, without obstructing Canada's progress.
I think that a country's progress rests, first of all, upon its human capital. And, among this human capital, more particularly the young people who will the more efficiently take over as they will be prepared to play their part.
It would not be proper standing up for the rights of the provinces and minorities to oppose the bill before us. To my mind this legislation respects provincial autonomy, because it recognizes, more particularly under clause 12, the exclusive right of the provinces in the educational field, and offers them the financial means of discharging their obligations with regard to those matters.
Under this bill, the federal government is not called upon to invest capital for educational purposes. It simply opens up a credit, because the money is lent by the banks, and not by the federal government. Thus, I think
Loans to Students
we may not claim that any adjustment could be made with the provinces, by resorting to the formula of equalization, at least not now.
The only sums of money that the federal government will have to disburse, are the interest payments. Clause 12 expressly provides that every province which would express this wish, be re-imbursed by the federal government for the interest it would have had to pay if such a province had been a party to the scheme. That is to my mind, the special status awarded, not to a single province, but to each of the 10 Canadian provinces which would want to do so, to be the only one to play a part in this assistance which is so much needed for our students, without obstructing the progress of Canada as a whole.
I understand that the province of Quebec will choose this option. With regard to this matter, I feel I am in good company with the Quebec premier when he states that he will not take part in this program, but will take up the option provided by clause 12 of the bill.
The Quebec premier understood that nothing in this legislation impinges upon the exclusive right of the provinces in matters of education. Moreover, this is a formula which enables each federal member to play the part entrusted to him by the people on the national level.

I was about to say that one exception to this rule is in a federal state where the provinces do not have control over customs duties and many other sources of revenue. Where the federation results in an accumulation of wealth in certain provinces which is drawn from the nation as a whole, that confederation is bound to change the pattern of the economy from what it would have been if the provinces making up the federation were separate entities. With that situation it is absolutely essential, I think, to have equalization payments of some sort so that there will be equality of opportunity in all parts of the country. There may also be other exceptions, but as a general principle I think it is a dangerous course of action for one level of government to collect the money which is going to be spent by another level of government.
I would think that this legislation would be welcomed in the province from which I come. I welcome it myself, and I say that because many of the people I represent are people with whom it has been a tradition for many years, even for centuries in some cases, to try to get a higher education if at all possible. It has been the custom for families to try to put at least one of their sons or daughters through university. There has been a thirst for higher education. I think this has been true generally in the maritimes. I am not excluding other parts of Canada but I believe that the maritime provinces have given a proportionately higher percentage of university trained people to North America generally, people who have been leaders in the professions, politics, the educational world and so on. I do not want to dwell on that point unduly, but for those who have a thirst for higher education and limited means to acquire it this legislation will certainly come as a welcome development.
I went through university during the depression and I know I would have welcomed such an opportunity as this very keenly when

I was going to college because I had to borrow most of the money involved, and it was a hard thing to do in those days.
In Prince Edward Island we have two main institutions of higher learning which have made great contributions to Canada in providing leaders in many fields from among their graduates. I refer to St. Dunstan's University and Prince of Wales college, which is a junior college; but many of the students in Prince Edward Island get part or all of their higher education in other provinces. To these students this legislation will be of great advantage, as in most cases the cost of education is higher to them, as they have to live away from home.
There are a few general questions for clarification purposes I wish to put to the minister. Perhaps he would make a note of them and give answers some time during the committee stage. One thing that concerns me is the application of the loans in the first year. As I see it, the situation that year will be a little different from what it will be after the scheme has been running for four or five years. I visualize that in the first year there will be applications from students who are doing postgraduate courses and this, in my judgment, would cut down the opportunities for other students who are in their undergraduate years. I am wondering what affect this may have or whether it will be of any great importance. It may be minor; I hope it is.
Then there is the matter raised by the hon. member for Edmonton West. I too wonder whether any study has been made of the effect of this program on applications by students for the R.O.T.P. program. I can visualize that the demand for these subsidized higher education courses might go down very considerably when this alternative method is available. I do not consider that as a defect in the legislation or in the scheme, but it might have a detrimental effect on the other program.
Also I am wondering what effect the granting of scholarships-I am thinking of special bursaries and so on-by the national research council, the Department of Fisheries and various other departments to aid students in universities will have on this legislation. If a student gets a scholarship, will this affect his ability to draw a loan?
I am also concerned with the question of the time of payment. I believe it is envisaged that the government will not hold itself liable for bad debts if the banks try to collect loans back in a period of less than five years. I would hope this would not prevent students who are in a position to do so from repaying
Loans to Students
their loans in a period less than five years, and that there would be no clause in the contracts requiring payments to extend over five years.
I am also wondering what calculation has been made of the effect this program will have on increased enrolment of university students in Canadian universities. It will do one of two things, or a combination of both. It will make the money available to people who are going to go to universities anyway. In that case it will not be very effective because if they are going anyway they will have financed themselves from somewhere. Or it will make these loans available to students who otherwise, without them, would not be able to go to university. I am wondering what is the estimate of increased enrolment in universities and what strain this will place on the facilities of the universities.
The minister has estimated that in a period of five years there will be $200 million to $250 million out on loan which, no doubt, is a fairly accurate estimate. But the amount out on loan will continue to increase for more than five years, depending on the length of period of repayment. It may increase for eight or nine years reaching a total of something like $400 million or $500 million. What is the significance of this from a financing point of view? Does this mean that the banks, by virtue of the fact that they will have half a billion dollars out on loan to students, will have their facilities to loan money to other people reduced by that amount, or does it mean that this will be new money that will be brought into the economy? If it is the latter I would point out that each year there will be a load of something like $25 million interest being paid to the banks by new graduates from the universities. I am not particularly objecting to that, but I would have hoped that a program of outright grants could have been introduced to cover this problem at least in part, if not entirely.
I have only one other reservation to express before I sit down. Having embarked on this scheme and when it has been in operation ten years, many young university graduates will be owing the banks a total sum of something like $500 million. At that time, or indeed at any time between now and then, it will be very difficult to introduce a system of scholarships or grants because these graduates will feel aggrieved that the new students will be getting for free what they had to borrow and are in the process of paying back with hard earned money. In practical terms, to introduce a scholarship system later

I think it would be necessary concurrently to forgive all or part of the outstanding debts of former graduates, and for that reason I see this legislation as an impediment to introducing a scholarship system of free grants to university students.

Mr. Chairman, education is too serious a matter for us to limit ourselves to passionate and emotional speeches. I simply wish to speak briefly on the problem before us.
We heard some members of the province of Quebec posing as police dogs for the province of Quebec, against the intrusion of the federal government in the field of education. Personally, I am against centralization through the federal government, and I am in favour of the provisions allowing the provinces to be respected in various fields, being adhered to by the federal government.
However, when we think that since confederation, such rights have been violated, have been taken away from the provinces, we must at least place ourselves in the proper context and finally take a decision concerning the legislation under study.
Mr. Chairman, I am opposed to the present monetary system, but this does not mean that I shall vote against all legislation being introduced in this house so long as social credit is not established in Canada. Such attitude would be ridiculous, and I find strange the attitude of those who feign the attitude of the offended virgin, and this, particularly when we know that the federal government pays grants through the national research council, that it awards scholarships through the various federal departments and that nobody objects to this. On the contrary, the universities, in brief, the students themselves -be they graduates or undergraduates, apply for scholarships to the national research council or various federal government departments.
Moreover, I remember very well that from 1936 to 1960, the Quebec premier was winning the elections by firmly refusing any grant from the federal government in the field of education. If this had improved the situation, I would have agreed with him but he was doing so merely to get elected. In fact, electors were saying: "Hon. Mr. Duplessis is opposed to all federal intrusion in provincial fields; Hon. Mr. Duplessis is in favour of autonomy; that is why we elect Mr. Duplessis." And today everyone regrets having elected him for such a long time.

Mr. Chairman, I know this is an intrusion into the field of education, but I am of the opinion that provincial business should remain under provincial jurisdiction.
During the study of the Columbia treaty, there have been many complaints that hon. members were trying to prevent the government of British Columbia from having what it wanted. The hon. members said at that time: "If the federal rights are protected, let us give to British Columbia the authorization it wants, because it is its business." In the province of Quebec, it is the same.
Personally, I am against certain decisions taken by the minister of education but this is my problem, it is my duty to settle it in Quebec, with the provincial authorities. I am a Quebec elector and if I am not satisfied with the Liberal government, I will turn it out.

-the only way of settling the problem was for the Ottawa government to hand over to Quebec, in the form of a fiscal equivalent, the amounts which it would have devoted to the repayment of interest on loans granted to students by banks and other institutions, taking into consideration the proportion pertaining to the Quebec population.

Jean Lesage, and he insisted that the federal government stick to those conditions. On July 14 the Minister of Finance, in his introduction of this bill on second reading, as appears at page 5442 of Hansard, stated the following:
Loans to Students
A university education or its vocational equivalent is the highest achievement of our educational system, and it should be within the financial grasp of every young Canadian who is capable of making good use of it.
These are some of the questions I would ask the minister to answer before we go any further in the deliberations of this bill. Can he explain to us what he had in mind by "vocational equivalent" of a university education? I think that would be of interest to many students and parents at this time.
Second, as I understand it the first year of university in some provinces commences after grade 12 high school. If that is the case then the students in those provinces will be eligible for a loan immediately after completing grade 12. Here again, in the province of Ontario we have a grade 13 in our high schools. If this bill does not apply to students in the province of Ontario until they enrol at university, then I think they are being discriminated against to the extent of that one year compared with the students from other provinces. Therefore I would ask the minister to set out what he has in mind in respect to this matter.
Might I also ask whether the minister anticipates an increase in enrolment at universities or institutions of higher education as a result of this legislation, and what is the estimated increase likely to be? Another question which comes to my mind is this. Suppose that a student obtains a loan for the first year at university and then obtains a loan for the second year. Then in the middle of the second year he drops out of school of his own volition but is unable to obtain work-which is quite possible because he would not have completed his education-in this event who will be responsible for the loan which had been made up to that time?
This is not a bill, Mr. Chairman, which we anticipated debating in the house as a result of promises which were made. Nevertheless we are prepared to pass it, because as I said earlier it is better than nothing. However, I do think that when this bill is passed it will preclude any scholarships in this country put forward by the federal government for many years to come.

In my opinion we have a right, now more than ever since this bill is under consideration, to seriously consider the way of interpreting a certain democratic formula used in our country.
I notice on page 5720 of Hansard for July 20 that the Minister of Finance stated:
I am not for a moment suggesting that majority opinion makes anything right but, by the same token, I certainly do not agree that minority opinion makes anything right either. The majority has some rights, even in this country.
Then he went on:
I suggest to my right hon. friend that this means in every country including Canada, particularly in Canada.
It is precisely because the majority has rights that the minorities have duties, and these duties consist in making sure that their rights are respected.
If, under the Canadian constitution, Quebec and the other provinces have exclusive rights in the field of education, I think that the representatives of the province of Quebec should, more than ever, show leadership in protecting those constitutional rights, especially in the field of education.
When we study how the other provinces have used their constitutional rights in the field of education as far as minorities are concerned, particularly their French speaking minorities, we appreciate how Quebec is anxious to keep its right to preserve and develop its culture through education, a right which is exclusively reserved to Quebec.
I would have expected a complete revision of the constitution, defining once and for all the rights of the provinces and those of

the federal government. But we have to make the best of what we have obtained up to now.
Under these arrangements, these agreements and even under this co-operative federalism, we are wondering, in the province of Quebec, if all this is not hypocrisy built up as a system in Canada and in the province of Quebec.
Federal-provincial conferences are held where official delegates of every provinces and the federal authorities meet. Then, we part company, and the day following these conferences, all the large newspapers of the two ethnical groups of this country-English and French newspapers-report on the complete failure of this or that federal-provincial conference. Then, after some secret meetings held between various departments, we are told that all is for the best in the best of all possible worlds; and two weeks later the same conference was called a tremendous fiasco.
I am wondering if that is not erecting legislative hyprocrisy into a system which is taking root, thanks to a Liberal government in Quebec as well as in Ottawa?
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I understand that the member for Quebec South (Mr. Cantin) should stand up for the minister and try to explain the paradoxical position taken by the premier of the province of Quebec who made a statement yesterday on this subject, saying that he disagreed with the bill, but nevertheless was accepting it since section 12 provides for alternative payments.
I understand that perhaps he owes something to the premier of the province of Quebec for sitting today in the house, even if he says he is the bearer of a Canadian mandate. I also understand that the premier of the province of Quebec has already received a Canadian mandate from the electorate. That is precisely under this mandate that he participated in the setting up of this federal centralizing policy, which he now seems to oppose.
I know that until we have a Social Credit government, we must participate in the present rehabilitation programs and serve the public interests in refusing to run the country into further debt. That is why, as soon as this bill was introduced, we presented an amendment requesting that the financing of this educational aid, which is needed by all the provinces, be achieved while respecting provincial rights.
When a member from Quebec tries to make a comparison to explain why he approves of this bill, saying that the students will be

able to benefit from federal scholarships, as did the hon. member from Quebec-Mont-morency (Mr. Marcoux), it must be remembered that there is a great difference between a federal scholarship which is a gift, a Quebec scholarship and a loan similar to those advocated in Bill No. C-110. It is not the same thing at all. It is not a scholarship to enable a student to continue his studies; it is just a loan, a way of getting into debt; that is why, as a member from the province of Quebec and the Social Credit party, I do not have the right to support this bill in any way, since it forces us, as members of parliament to get into debt another group of people which had yet to fall into the federal government's clutches.
As a second reason, we must take into consideration the respect that Quebec citizens jealously demand from the federal government even if the latter succeeded, through broadcasting, to have admitted the principle that the federal government had rights in the field of education. Even if they succeeded, through the Canada Council and the Massey commission to have certain facts accepted by the province of Quebec, I think this bill, even if it provides for alternative payments, as an exception for the province of Quebec, has nothing in common with the promise of scholarships to be granted by the province of Quebec to further free education, but it is rather related to a system of bank loans.
That is quite a difference between free education promised by the officer responsible for education in the province of Quebec, the minister of education, or between the version given by the premier of the province of Quebec concerning free education at all levels and his paradoxical acceptance in the statement he made last night.
I do not think that we, not as representatives of the province of Quebec, but simply as Canadians, could accept this bill because the representative of the Conservative party in the province of Quebec as well as those of the Ralliement Creditiste strongly objected to the bill from a constitutional point of view, because it is a direct interference in a field where the people of the province of Quebec will be more than ever jealous of the rights given to them by the constitution.

It is exactly the kind of speeches which breed separatism in some regions of Canada, especially in the province of Quebec.
Mr. Chairman, hon. members should understand the province of Quebec and make much of it, because French Canadians are a minority in Canada and North America. The stronger Quebec will be and the more the provincial jurisdictions will be respected and the more the autonomy of Quebec is respected, the more satisfied, will be the citizens of Quebec, and then we will have a more closely united Canada. It must not be forgotten that the province of Quebec acts as a brake to the annexation of Canada to United States, because it has a different language and culture from other provinces. We would be the first ones to object to our annexation to the United States, because we wish to keep our culture, our language and our rights.
Mr. Chairman, the students of Quebec are not the only ones to object strongly to this bill. There are also some associations of students in English speaking provinces.

The president of the students' association of the University of Toronto, Mr. John Roberts, asserts that the federal legislation providing loans for students will not help those who are in greatest need of financial assistance. Referring to the legislation which enables students to borrow up to $1,000 a year from any chartered bank, while the federal government guarantees the loan and pays the interest, Mr. Roberts pointed out that it will benefit science students at the expense of art students who get paid lower salaries after completing their studies.

This shows that when the federal government interferes in a field outside its own jurisdiction, it often creates inconveniences and problems. And in this case, as I pointed out, the president of the students' association of the University of Toronto is raising objections regarding this legislation.
Mr. Chairman, this bill is a new type of co-operative federalism. It must be borne in mind that the St. Jean Baptiste society federation termed co-operative federalism national suicide. When advantage is taken of this disguised formula to interfere in an exclusively provincial field, co-operative federalism is a policy of division, because there is an option formula. By giving a choice to any province that wants it, the government recognizes thereby that the bill is unconstitutional. If the federal government actually saw fit to include an option in this legislation, it is because it is unacceptable under the constitution. The nine English speaking provinces do not object to an intrusion of the federal government in the educational field, because the majority is English speaking as in Ottawa. Such is not the case in the province of Quebec and this is why such a violation of the Canadian constitution is so serious, because the province of Quebec is not a province like the others.
It seems to me that, by granting an option under this bill, the federal government condemns itself and admits that this bill is ultra vires. We would be very happy to know the opinion of the Minister of Justice, and to know whether he shares the view I am expressing at the present time, namely that the very fact of granting an option to the provinces, if desired, constitutes an admission that the bill is ultra vires and that the federal government is dealing with problems which do not concern itj in brief, that this bill represents an encroachment on the jurisdiction of the provinces.
Mr. Chairman, I do not think that we are resorting to dishonest tactics, as stated by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher), when we demand respect for the Canadian constitution each time the federal government enters or intrudes into a field of provincial jurisdiction, from which it never withdraws. On the contrary, it goes on interfering more all the time. This bill constitutes a policy of separation, of division, which is contrary, in my opinion, to the principles of national unity.

It seems, Mr. Chairman, that only members of the Ralliement Creditiste are against this measure and are not trying to find any excuse to allow the government to enter into this field. They seem to be the only ones who are unwilling to let their province be crucified, not even on a golden cross. This makes me wonder where are the Quebec representatives in the other parties, and especially those who try, much to the annoyance of their colleagues from other provinces, to pose as champions of the French fact within the two old-line parties, as in the Social Credit party sitting to our right.
But before explaining in my fashion the reasons why my colleagues and myself are indomitably against this bill, I must admit that, as was said earlier, we are not against the principle of the bill. As a matter of fact, one would have to be blind or unfair to fail to recognize that young people through-

out the country need help to be able to reach and attend university and complete higher studies.
I admit that today education is not a luxury, but actually a great need. I suspect that those unable to attend university or institutions of higher learning will face more and more a very dismal future, especially if nothing is changed in our present educational system.
I understand that the legislation now under consideration is meant to redress social injustice existing for so long and which only enabled the wealthy families to send their children to university. I also understand that there is an urgent need for the country to promote education in order to have a greater number of scientists, of engineers, in all branches, physicians, lawyers, notaries, and highly qualified businessmen.
We have to hasten to make up for lost time and to keep ourselves up to date with the rapid development of science. In short, we admit these facts and we wish one day that the only standards required from those who would like to attend university would be the ability, the necessary qualifications and not the financial means.
But what we, members of the Ralliement Creditistes, do not admit is the method used to reach that objective.
I do not admit it because it is an attempt to interfere to a greater extent in the field of education.
The tragedy I mentioned at the beginning is precisely that abnormal fact which makes everyone say: It is a provincial field, a provincial right recognized by all, but only members of the Ralliement Creditistes strongly protest against its violation, except possibly-and I must add to their great merit-some Conservative members from Quebec.

The federal government occupies fields of taxation which belong to the provinces; it levies certain sums of money which should be levied by the provinces, then offers the provincial governments to spend that money in such and such a field.
This is what is unconstitutional and, moreover, it is intrinsically bad and dangerous when it concerns education. Mr. Chairman, when the house adjourned at six o'clock I was about to make a few suggestions to the Minister of Finance with regard to Bill No. C-110 which we are now considering.

After all the discussion-there have been many speeches-the Minister of Finance must have noticed a difference between the province of Quebec and the other provinces, because all the other provinces are ready to accept the bill as it is, or perhaps with a few unimportant amendments. But we, from the province of Quebec, are unable to accept it, even with all the good will in the world.
Many opinions have been expressed and many requests have been made to the Minister of Finance. Moreover, many speeches have been made by hon. members from our group, as well as by other French Canadian members who wish to defend the cause of the province of Quebec in this house. Then came the requests from Quebec university students, in support of what we were saying here in this house.
I would point out to the minister that we sincerely believed he would be bringing us a few minor amendments. We have not proposed any at this stage, because we can feel that the great majority are in favour of this bill and we do not want to impose lengthy speeches upon the hon. members. However, it is absolutely essential that the minister take some action to prevent the prolonged and accelerated disagreement of the province of Quebec, within confederation, due to the attitude of the present government.
Today the minister seemed to insist upon the statement made by Hon. Jean Lesage, premier of the province of Quebec. I was wondering why the Minister of Finance seemed so sure of his opinions. I see now that he has met the Quebec premier. After having read in Le Devoir that the Quebec premier had stated that Quebec would not take part in the federal system of loans to students, I was quite glad. At first, I was pleased with the title. But when I read further on that he had said that he would rather take advantage of the option formula which would enable him to receive an alternative payment, I immediately disapproved that attitude. It is this crucial point which has prompted our objection to the bill now under study. When the Quebec premier stated: "I will not take part in the federal program of loans to students, but I will accept the sums given by the federal government as a compensation", we had to show our disapproval.
Mr. Chairman, it should be borne in mind that mankind was doomed once because of a forbidden fruit, and I believe this is the forbidden fruit that Mr. Lesage should never have accepted.
Loans to Students
This afternoon, the Minister of Finance told us that the Quebec premier stands for the province of Quebec. I agree that Mr. Lesage stands for the province of Quebec for a certain time, and maybe not for long; but I no longer agree with him when he says that Mr. Lesage stands for the majority of the people of Quebec. I would even go so far as to say that French Canadian members of the Liberal party share this opinion, because after all is said, when we receive something from the federal government, it is because the latter collected it in our province under the guise of taxes to return a part of it to us.
I see the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Deschatelets) who shakes his head and I ask him if it is for that reason. I wonder how he cannot possibly admit that this is an intrusion by the federal government when it is said that compensation payments will be given back to the province of Quebec. Necessarily, those compensation payments come from taxes paid by the province of Quebec, there is no argument about it.
If we refuse to accept those compensation payments, the federal government will not be able to levy taxes in the province on account of those compensation payments. We want to prevent the government from opening this gap so as to rob again the province of Quebec.
I said previously in several of my speeches that we were old enough to levy our own taxes. We do not need the federal government to levy those taxes and then to give us back the amount collected. We are old enough to do that and we need those taxes to protect our rights.
That is exactly what I want to blame the federal government for. The premier says that the province of Quebec will not participate in that loans scheme but if the federal government gives it something, it follows that it will get it back through the back door.
I might be going against the premier of Quebec in that respect but I am happy to do so because he is violating the constitution. It is more serious for a provincial premier to do that than for a private member of the House of Commons.
I heard the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Cantin) say that we are federal administrators and legislators and that we must act as Canadians.
Well, I am here in Canada as a "Canadian French Canadian" and I defend the province of Quebec in this parliament. No one can stop

Loans to Students
me from doing so any more than I can stop an Anglo-Saxon from defending his English speaking province.
That is why, at the outset of my remarks, I said that I fully agree with any province which is in favour of this bill. However, if that does not suit the province of Quebec, we just have to make a small amendment with which the Minister of Finance is familiar to replace the alternative payments by a tax abatement of some kind-0.5 or 0.9 per cent- in favour of any province which withdraws from the scheme. Everybody would agree, nobody could say that we are violating the constitution. I believe the minister must have given serious thought to it as he is much more qualified than I am in this respect. I wonder now what is preventing him from taking an initiative of this kind.
Instead of having these alternative payments, we could return a certain percentage of the taxation rights to the province of Quebec. It seems to me it would be much easier to do this than to do what was agreed upon with the provincial minister, who is a former Ottawa centralizer-we know him.
I suggest that, should the Minister of Finance consider this little amendment, everybody will agree with him. Moreover, he will make many friends in the province of Quebec.
On the other hand, when we blame Mr. Jean Lesage for accepting this bill, he states: "I cannot possibly send the provincial police in the other provinces". That is not what we ask of him. He should leave the other provinces in peace, as the other provinces leave him in peace, but he should look after his province and cease to play "trust", even on a small scale.
We are not meddling in the affairs of other provinces, the hon. members are aware of that. But our only protection is the constitution. We are told that this bill does not violate the constitution. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to draw the attention of the committee very briefly to certain implications of the Canada student loan legisla-
Loans to Students
tion. This bill provides for student loans to a maximum of $1,000 a year for a maximum of five years at a "specified educational institution", that is, one offering courses at the post-secondary school level. When a student has ceased to be a full time student for seven months he is liable for payment of interest or principal on the $5,000.
Let us examine some of the possible consequences of this situation. No student can be expected to finance a university education on the maximum of $1,000 a year and if a student must drop out for a year to earn enough to further his education his loan will fall due in the midst of his efforts and his education will be delayed even further. A student who ceases to qualify academically for the loan and must drop out to work will face the same problem. This is a severe obstruction to the intended purpose of the bill.
Let us then consider the successful student who completes his education on student loans. Those who find good jobs on graduation will experience no difficulty in paying their debts. However if a student should wish to pursue graduate studies, medicine or dentistry it will be virtually impossible for him to do so. Such studies are expensive enough without the added burden of a loan repayment. Medical students pay from one half to two thirds more than other university students and dental students pay even more.
At the moment our graduate students comprise only 0.6 per cent of the student age population compared with 1.4 per cent in the United States. In this country, where young people are not required to spend time in the armed forces, they should be making a far better showing than this. Yet we choose this time to provide effective discouragement.
The Hall commission report has stated that by 1971 we will need 7,100 new doctors and 2,130 new dentists. The medical and dental graduates of 1971 are entering university this year or have already entered. Those who choose to pursue medical or dental careers will be prevented from or delayed in doing so if they should take advantage of loans now.
One grave deficiency of the legislation is the failure to provide loans for students beyond the undergraduate level. Not only does it fail to provide for these students but it offers direct discouragement. The terms of the bill must be changed and clarified so that students proceeding beyond the undergraduate level will be exempt from payment of interest or principal while their formal studies continue. During this period, as during

Loans to Students
the undergraduate period, the government should continue to accept responsibility for the interest payments. Furthermore, new legislation must be introduced immediately to provide direct financial aid for students at this level, as recommended by the Hall commission report.
The government has made a faltering step in the direction of student aid and perhaps we should not scorn it, but they must not be allowed to believe that they have done enough. The program of scholarships we heard so much about at election time has vanished and has been replaced by a scheme that may do more harm than good in the long run. It is one more in the series of government attempts to make it appear that they are taking adequate action on our most serious problems. They know it is inadequate and they must not be allowed to forget this.
To state that loans will give the student the feeling of having earned his way to an education and that scholarships are somehow equivalent to charity is ludicrous. Any intelligent student who works hard enough to gain a scholarship deserves it and has most certainly earned his way. This must not be used as an excuse to avoid scholarships any longer.
We need not only a broader loan program but scholarships and bursaries of all kinds to provide the doctors, dentists, nurses, medical teachers and other professional people we need so badly. We must not settle for stopgap measures.

The purpose of the amendment is to remedy a constitutional defect in the bill which I endeavoured to point out to the house in the debate on second reading on July 15. Without the amendment, I confidently assert, and much more confidently since the debate in this house took place, that the legislation contains a fatal defect which renders it invalid and unconstitutional unless this or some similar amendment is made. Parliament is sometimes described, Mr. Chairman, as a court. I imagine there is no court in the world in which it is less appropriate to make a lengthy legal argument. I will not repeat what I said on second reading the other day; I will just try to summarize the point for any members who were not present on that occasion and who do not read Hansard.
The point is that clause 2 (b), and indeed clause 2 (k) as well, delegate to the lieutenant governor in council, that is to say the provincial cabinet, the right to designate the appropriate authorities who are to have the power to grant certificates of eligibility. Without a certificate of eligibility, you do not get a loan and the whole legislation falls to the ground. The authorities who designate the people who get these certificates are the lieutenant governors in council. The delegation by this parliament to the provincial executive which is set up by the British North America Act and not subordinate in any sense to this parliament is in my view the delegation of a legislative power, and in accordance with the principle laid down by the Supreme Court of Canada in the Nova Scotia Interdelegation Conference case, is an unauthorized and invalid delegation.
The parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance made a very courteous and disarming speech in answer to the remarks I made on this matter. I thank him, and indeed I thank the Minister of Finance for their kind references to me in the debate. I must say that as I listened to their words I felt very much like counsel before a judge who hears the judge start his remarks by saying, "I have listened to the very able argument of counsel for the defendant", and who then proceeds to dismiss his case. It is always bad when you hear words of praise coming from those who are trying to persuade. I do not intend to be diverted, Mr. Chairman, by the kind words and able arguments of the parliamentary secretary in support of the constitutionality of this bill.

They only served to reinforce my conviction that the legislation as it now stands, without amendment, is in fact unconstitutional.
I noticed that the hon. member for Royal, who I hope will speak later in this discussion and who is a former attorney general of one of the provinces, supported my argument. I may say that I have spoken to many other learned members of the house-I will not embarrass them by naming them-who have expressed to me at least the same opinion I advanced. The parliamentary secretary said that the Nova Scotia case dealt with delegation by parliament to the legislatures and vice-versa from the legislatures to parliament, and did not deal with delegation from parliament to the provincial cabinet or vice-versa. Of course, this is so. This is very obvious; but as I pointed out in my previous remarks this is a difference and not a distinction.
It will not have escaped the notice of the parliamentary secretary that at least one of the judges in the Nova Scotia case, Mr. Justice Kellock, made no distinction of this sort and referred to both the executive and the legislature delegation in the same breath, as it were. Nor is there any point, at least in my view, in the suggestion that the lieutenant governor's duties are administrative in nature, which is one of the main arguments presented by the parliamentary secretary. The fact is that the duties of the lieutenant governor are spelled out by the British North America Act. They cannot be added to by parliament. What opinion, I ask you, would be advanced if the provincial legislatures passed an act, without the consent of this parliament, purporting to delegate powers, duties and responsibilities to the governor general in council? The situation would be precisely the same.
As I have said, the parliamentary secretary said that the legislation only delegates administrative authority to the provincial cabinet. I think the parliamentary secretary knows better than that. An administrative duty can, in fact, be delegated. An administrative duty is one which is not discretionary in its nature. Indeed, the standards and details are spelled out by the legislation, leaving only the administrative application to the administrator. If the parliamentary secretary wants authority for that statement I would refer him to the case of Bridge v. The Queen in 1953 Supreme Court Reports. In the present legislation the whole responsibility for selecting the authorities to grant certificates of eligibility is left to the lieutenant governor in council.

The standard of selection is not suggested. The same applies to the selection of the institutions of learning to be covered by the act under clause 2(k). This is left wide open. There is complete discretion in this field, as the Minister of Finance has already pointed out several times in this debate.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that it would be the height of irresponsibility to refuse to amend the defect I have pointed out, even if some hon. members may think I am wrong. The minister and the parliamentary secretary were both kind enough to suggest that in this particular field my opinion, even though they did not agree with it, was entitled to consideration. If that is so, Mr. Chairman, does it not make sense to seek to remedy the defect even if they are not sure it exists? There is a Latin maxim familiar to some, ex abundanti cautela, which means that if there is a defect or a suggested defect you meet it whether you have to do so or not. I suggest that common sense priciples of draftsmanship should be adopted by the government.
I am trying to salvage this bill from the constitutional wreckers. After listening to my hon. friend, the member for Danforth, I was not so sure the measure deserved to be salvaged. But I would have thought that the people who put forward this legislation in the house and who have spoken in glowing terms of its effects would be the very first ones to welcome with open arms an amendment calculated to remove reasonable doubts, and I suggest these are at least reasonable doubts, as to the constitutional validity.
I quote the parliamentary secretary from page 5576 of Hansard. He is referring to what I had said in the previous debate, and says:
I should not ignore the fact that the learned member proposed an alternative method-
I ask the committee to note these words.
-and in my very humble opinion that alternative was valid and did not affect the fabric of the bill.
If that is so, if the suggestion is valid, if there is a reasonable doubt, and it is admitted there is a reasonable doubt, then I suggest it is pretty obvious that the gap should be plugged and the defect remedied.
What a laughingstock would be made of the government and, what is much worse, of this parliament if we pass this legislation and then the banks refuse to make loans because they say it has not been passed constitutionally, just because we have failed to accept a reasonable amendment that will clear up the doubt. Incidentally the banks have very competent

legal advisers, and I wonder whether the government has secured any opinion from these advisers as to the constitutionality of the particular point I am raising.
The Minister of Finance says: This is a legal problem and it is difficult to be sure who is right; we think we are right and if we are wrong let the courts decide. I do not like to say anything harsh to the Minister of Finance-perhaps it does not matter as at the moment he is not listening

but does he not think it is irresponsible to fail to remedy defects that can be remedied by simple amendment, especially when, if this legislation is held to be defective, many students will be grievously disappointed by this parliament?
I move an amendment, Mr. Chairman, the substance of which is to say that in lieu of the selection of these agencies or authorities by the lieutenant governors in council, which I say is unconstitutional, the delegation shall be to the governor general in council, in regard to whom we clearly have the power, upon the recommendation of the lieutenant governors in council. This will give the same authority to the lieutenant governors in council, will leave provincial rights intact in fact and will plug a constitutional gap. I say that if this amendment is not accepted and if the advice that has been proffered from this side of the house is declined, a very heavy responsibility will rest upon the government for refusing to accept this reasonable amendment.

Mr. Chairman, the committee will appreciate my difficulty inasmuch as I did not become acquainted with the technical and difficult arguments put forth by the hon. member for Greenwood until they fell from his lips. Consequently I rise with my side bleeding from the spur of the moment. May I say I enter into the lists because I do not wish to offend the constitutional consciences of the hon. members for Greenwood and Royal.
Allow me to say, after listening to the arguments put forth with unusual skill and ability by the hon. member for Greenwood, I still do not despair of the constitutional purity of the clause. Dealing with this matter with appropriate brevity, I would remind myself and the committee of the admonition of Chief Justice Taschereau when he said the court is not concerned with the arguments set out in Hansard when determining constitutional points raised before the supreme court.
As I understood the hon. member for Greenwood, he assailed me most strongly because I stated this was an administrative and not a legislative act. As I understand the law, an administrative act is one more specific in scope, dealing with specific individuals and not dealing with the public in general, and I took comfort in my position from the statement found in the authoritative book "Administrative Law" by H. W. R. Wade. I am reading textually from page 249:
There is only a hazy borderline between legislation and administration, and the assumption that they are two fundamentally different forms of power is misleading.

He went on to say on the same page:
It is easy to see that legislative power is the power to lay down the law for people in general, whereas administrative power is the power to lay down the law for them individually, or in some particular case.
The hon. member for Greenwood opened up his attack by stating there was no discretion given to a person carrying out an administrative act. May I, with great respect to the hon. member and the committee, draw attention to page 250 of the same text where it states:
But where, as happens so frequently, such legislation can be properly administered only by constantly adjusting it to the needs of the situation, allowed.
It is my humble submission, looking at the scope of this bill, that I find no reason to retreat from my position that this is an administrative act which we are delegating to the lieutenant governor in council.

Where an accused Is, pursuant to this Part, found to be insane, the lieutenant governor of the province may make an order for the safe custody of the accused in the place and in the manner that he may direct.

The lieutenant governor of any province may from time to time make regulations for the purpose of preventing escapes and preserving discipline in the case of prisoners in any common jail or prison employed beyond the limits of such common jail or prison.
That again I say is another illustration of the parliament of Canada giving authority to the lieutenant governors in council. Under that section they are empowered to make regulations and it is my humble submission that this is a clear illustration of the principle I am putting to the committee.
May I also invite the attention of the committee to a rather interesting pamphlet I have here referring to the law on the office of the lieutenant governor of a province. I would like to refer the committee to the commission that is given to a lieutenant governor and, if I may, I wish to read the material parts:
We have reposed in you, according to the several powers, provisions and directions granted or appointed you by virtue of the Act of the Parliament of the United Kingdom... known as "British North America Act, 1867,"-
Then it goes on and says:
-or which may from time to time be given to you, in respect of the said province of... under the sign manual of Our Governor General of Canada or by order of our privy council for Canada-
And it goes on and says further:
-and according to such laws as are or may be in force within the said province-
It is my position, Mr. Chairman, that the lieutenant governor obtains his power from three sources. He gets it under the British North America Act; he gets it according to the commission from the powers given to him from time to time under the sign manual of the governor in council or by order of the privy council, and third-and this is the pertinent part of the argument I am putting forth-
-according to such laws as are or may be in force within the said province-

I suggest those words were deliberately chosen and carefully framed. You will note they do not say the laws of the province, but from the laws within the province. Therefore in my submission, if this bill is enacted it will become the law within the province and will delegate power to the lieutenant governor in council which can be constitutionally accepted and exercised within the commission granted to the lieutenant governor.
Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to detain the committee unduly. As I indicated earlier, whatever arguments we may make here are not in any event binding on the court which may have to rule on the constitutional point. It is my submission that this is a legislative act which can be properly delegated to the lieutenant governor in council, and I trust I will be acquitted of any disrespect to the hon. member for Greenwood when I invite the committee to reject his amendment.
