May I say to the committee in support of the bill as proposed by the Minister of Finance that when this provision was drafted in its present form it was drafted in accordance with the spirit of the discussions and basic arrangements which had been made with the provinces.
There has been much argument to the effect that possibly, although I do not admit it myself, this legislation goes too directly to the sphere of education. It was felt that to the extent that local jurisdiction or administrative action could be retained the more it would be in keeping with the whole spirit of the discussions and the arrangements which were made, bearing in mind that the members of this house believe it is essential in the interest of Canada that loans be made available on a national basis to Canadian students.
Before translating into the present bill this situation in which the lieutenant governor in council in each province would at his discretion, after proper investigation, designate the proper authority, care was taken to ascertain that full jurisdiction was vested in the federal parliament. It did occur to the legal advisers of the crown that in 1951, in the Nova Scotia case to which the hon. member for Greenwood referred, it was clearly decided that there could not be an exchange of legislative powers between the parliament of Canada and the legislatures of the provinces, and vice-versa. This only means that section 92 of the British North America Act states that when laws in relation to one subject may be made by the legislature of a province the province may not transfer to Canada its jurisdiction to legislate in this respect.
I agree with the hon. member for Greenwood and others who have spoken on this point, that we should not transform this House of Commons into a forum for legal and legalistic debate. But just for the information of the members of the house I would say that we have fully considered the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in 1952 in the case concerning the potato marketing board, which is reported in the Supreme Court Reports for that year at page 392 and the following pages. It was fully considered that in that case the matter of delegation from one legislature or from parliament to a provincial body or organism chosen as the agent of that legisla-

tive body was accepted as constitutional and distinguishable from the situation in the other case to which reference has been made. In other words, when section 91-

subtopic: MEASURE TO FACILITATE MAKING LOANS TO STUDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there is one point which I believe has not been considered and which strikes at the very basis of the arguments which have been so forcefully presented. I think the main point of the bill is the definition of who is entitled to receive a loan. We find it in paragraph (e) of clause 2. I am not anticipating this paragraph because it is directly connected with this particular point. My hon. friend from Queens-Lunenburg intends to raise this matter on the next paragraph in another connection. Clause 2(e) reads:
"Certificate of eligibility" means a certificate... issued by an appropriate authority-
That authority is the authority we are now considering. It is the authority which has to decide which student is in need of a loan. I believe this is the heart of the legislation, the substantive part. Someone has to define which student is in need of a loan to be provided under this bill. These words "to be in need of a student loan" are not defined anywhere in the bill. Furthermore, Mr. Chairman, there is no power presently granted to the governor in council to define which person is in need of a student loan and which person is not. In other words, the bill is completely silent as to who can apply for, and who is in need of, a student loan. There is no power in the governor in council to make such a definition, and I have gone through clause 13 very carefully.
In these circumstances we are left with the situation that the authority we are now discussing is going to have to define what

amounts to the very heart of this bill, namely who is in need of a student loan. The hon. member for Greenwood and the hon. member for Royal raised arguments which were countered by the answer that this was something in the nature of an administrative problem. But it is necessary to have the certifying authority define who is in need of a student loan. I submit it goes much beyond an administrative act and actually becomes a legislative act. I think this is one of the most serious problems which the government will have to face in trying to determine whether this certifying authority will be going beyond its constitutional powers.
This is slightly out of sequence, but it is a very important part of the bill and I think makes the arguments already raised by other hon. members much more valid. We are not dealing merely with something which is defined in the bill and which must be administered. Each province will have to define who is in need of a student loan. As I see it, each province will have to set up a means test, if that is what is required, and will have to decide that one person is in need of a loan while another is not. I think this is very basic to this legislation. Furthermore, the situation would vary from province to province unless a definition is given by this bill or unless some central authority is able to co-ordinate it.
The suggestion made by the hon. member for Greenwood in his amendment is that the Governor General should make this definition on the recommendation of the lieutenant governor. It seems logical that that should be done because in this case he can also define who is in need of a student loan. I think that very serious consideration should be given this particular matter before we go any further with this amendment.

The minister says "not at all". When we were discussing credit unions the minister pointed out that this was banking legislation; that he did not want to do anything which might interfere with it because it was banking legislation; that he did not want to get into provincial jurisdiction. I agree with him about its being banking legislation. I have always taken the position that this legislation is similar to the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the Small Businesses Loans Act, the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, and so on. This is legislation to guarantee bank loans and it comes solely within federal jurisdiction. Then the Minister of Justice gets up tonight and says that, while he is not admitting it, we are now giving these powers to the lieutenant governor in council because there may be a feeling that this really has to do with education.
I wonder whether the members have thought through what is involved in both paragraph (b) and paragraph (k). This parliament is going to guarantee loans to students, but the right to determine the basis upon which those loans will be made to students and the right to determine which institutions shall be considered educational institutions is going to lie exclusively within a provincial body not responsible to the Minister of Finance, but responsible to the lieutenant governor in council of the province.
This, as the minister himself admitted, is a permissive paragraph. The lieutenant governor in council does not have to set up the eligibility authority at all. Or a provincial cabinet could take office which might decide to dismiss the eligibility authority, in which case loans would not be available in that province. This has surely departed a long way from banking legislation. We have not done this under any other loans legislation. Under this legislation the minister is now saying that while the government is going to guarantee loans, the determination as to who will get these loans, under what circumstances the students will get them and the kind of institutions they will have to attend in order to get them will lie with the lieutenant governor in council. It seems to me that this is a great departure from banking legislation.
Now, we laymen are not expected to get into the deep, constitutional arguments that lawyers enjoy. However, laymen, Mr. Chairman, at least know that when the lieutenant governor of a province sits down to pass orders in council they are passed on the basis

Loans to Students
of a provincial statute. The preamble of the order in council must state the statute under which that order in council is passed. Here we say the lieutenant governor in council may pass an order in council on the basis of a federal statute. It seems to me that to make absolutely sure, one of two things has to be done.
We can do as has been done with marketing and other joint legislative fields, that is have the province also pass an act giving to the legislative authority certain powers delegated by this parliament. The lieutenant governor in council can pass an order in council under authority of that provincial statute, using the authority delegated by this parliament. The disadvantage of following that procedure is that most legislatures will not meet until next winter. This legislation should become effective this fall so a student can borrow money to go to university this year.
The other alternative is the one which has been proposed by the hon. member for Greenwood, namely that the governor general in council appoint these boards. This seems to me to be more logical. These boards should be responsible to the governor general in council. The regulations should be passed by the governor general in council and the boards should be responsible to the Minister of Finance. They should be appointed by the governor general in council on the recommendation of the provincial cabinet. It seems to me that this is the proper and logical way to proceed, irrespective of the fact the Minister of Justice can find a potato case in Prince Edward Island that gives some hope this bill might get by.
The fact remains that if there is any doubt at all this committee ought to make sure this legislation will stand up. Even if there is no constitutional objection, and we think there is, I for one would take very serious objection to legislation passed by this parliament being inapplicable in any province where the lieutenant governor in council merely chooses not to appoint the eligibility authority or decides to discontinue the eligibility authority. If a province wants, under clause 12, to come under the alternative payments section, then that is fine. However, under this paragraph (b) the province that failed to make the appointment of an eligibility authority could make this bill inapplicable in that province.

NORTHERN AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: REPORTED INTENTION TO CARRY OUT RAILROAD SURVEY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question I asked today had to do with the exploitation of some 20 billion tons of iron in a deposit which straddles the boundary of the Yukon and the Northwest Territories in the vicinity of Snake river. It is my understanding that the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources has made an announcement outside of the house of a cooperative effort that is going to be made to survey a railroad route through the Yukon territory to the Snake river property. I understand also that there will be an involvement by the Canadian National Railways and by the company which owns the mineral claims in the Yukon and Northwest Territories where these properties are located.

I want to ask the minister to explain as fully as he is able at this moment, consistent with all circumstances as to the security of the interests of the government and of the company involved, the plans with respect to this survey and to forecast, if he can and as far as he can, the plans of the government in the future.
Specifically I would like to ask the minister whether or not his department has been in communication with the White Pass and Yukon railroad with respect to the conversion of that railroad to standard gauge, because I would assume any railroad to be constructed to the Snake river property would be of standard gauge. I might say in closing these brief remarks that a railroad is, of course, an absolute necessity if a deposit of this size is to be exploited economically and to compete with other sources.
It is my hope this deposit could be brought into production within the next decade. Certainly this iron ore deposit, which is estimated as being the largest in the free world, will contribute in no uncertain terms to the national economy of Canada as a whole, and would be of particular interest to the development of resources generally in the Yukon and Northwest Territories. I need not add that the construction of any railroad through the Mayo area to Snake river would be a tremendous advantage for the full exploitation of the extensive mineral potential which is known to exist in this particular area, and of which I am sure the minister is well aware.

Undoubtedly this tremendous asset will be developed some day and it is in the interests of Canada that it be developed at as early a time as possible. The company has gone to some considerable extent, involving expenditure of some $2 or $3 million including assess-20220-367
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion ment of the feasibility of a pipe line, because this area is some 421 miles from water. At the present time iron ore is in a buyers' market but this will not always continue, and various estimates up to 10 years have been made for bringing the deposit into production.
I want to assure the hon. member that we did talk to the Yukon and White Pass, they being the pioneer railway people there, as we thought anything I had to say on the matter might possibly have an immediate reflection on their own activities, and before I uttered the few words in Edmonton we did get in touch with Mr. Frank Browne of that railway. AGRICULTURE-PROVISION OF FEED LOT FOR SASKATCHEWAN CATTLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question which I directed this afternoon to the Minister of Agriculture was in reference to the statement he made yesterday in regard to the drought stricken areas of Saskatchewan. He stated that about 2,500 cattle had been put into community pastures, and other steps were being taken; but there is one matter he did not mention and that is that in about a month's time the farmers will be faced with the problem of taking their cattle to the market.
I would remind him of what happened in 1961 when we had a similar drought in Saskatchewan. There were more cattle on the market than the market could absorb, as a result of which prices were forced down to the extent that the cattle brought in only about half as much as they would usually make at that time of the year. But on that occasion the government set up feed lots. The cattle which the market could not absorb were put into these feed lots and fed at government expense until such time as the market could again absorb them. This is exactly what 1 would like to have the Minister of Agriculture

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion be prepared to do. In about a month's time some of these cattle which farmers may not be able to keep on their hands owing to a shortage of feed will again appear on these markets. I do not wish this to be a case of "too little and too late", because any such arrangement as I have suggested will have to be undertaken in conjunction with the provincial governments before feed lots can be established.
It may be said there is still a month in which to act. But the minister made no mention of any such proposal in his statement, and since there was no word that it had been discussed with the Saskatchewan minister of agriculture I took it for granted that it had been overlooked. It is my contention that unless immediate steps are taken and discussions begun with the ministers of agriculture in the prairie provinces to find ways of dealing with this situation, then the farmers who will have to send their cattle to the markets will again have to sell their livestock at fire sale prices.

maintopic: NATIONAL PARKS-REGULATIONS PROHIBITING MINORS UNACCOMPANIED BY ADULTS
NATIONAL PARKS-REGULATIONS PROHIBITING MINORS UNACCOMPANIED BY ADULTS
speechtext:
The question I directed to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources this morning was prompted by representations from various councillors and interested individuals in the counties of Essex and Kent, and dealt particularly with the national park known as the Pelee national park.
Because of recent cases of vandalism in the park the superintendent of the park found it necessary to put in some stringent regulations to the effect that no minors could enter the park for camping purposes unless accompanied by an adult.
As one who spent most of his life growing up in the shadow of Point Pelee national park, I am quite familiar with the park. I know it is one of our smallest national parks and that there is a tremendous influx of people, especially in the summertime, on weekdays and week ends. I know that it is an extremely difficult task to police this park adequately, because of these conditions. But the imposition of a regulation to the effect that minors cannot be admitted for camping purposes unless accompanied by an adult does work undue hardship on a great number of children from the Essex and Kent county areas who would normally go to this park to spend two days, a week or two weeks camping. There are excellent camping facilities in this park, and have been for a number of years, and the park itself is ideal for the younger generation.
My request to the minister today was for him to see whether something could not be done to police this park adequately, so that these regulations might be modified to the degree that children unaccompanied by adults may once again go into the park. The matter is urgent, sir, because this is the time of the school holidays and there are only approximately six weeks left in which a great many children could avail themselves of this opportunity. Certainly it is a case, once more, where a majority of well disciplined children are being made to suffer for the irresponsible acts of a very few. It is my hope that the minister, having received all these delegations and requests, will have had time to look into this matter and can perhaps come up with a feasible solution that might adequately solve this entire problem to the satisfaction of all concerned.
